title: The midwives (Exodus 1)
hook: Shiphrah and Puah refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the boys

segments.voice: Yesterday, providence: you thought evil, but God turned it to good, and Genesis closed. Your line was god turned it to good. Today a new book opens: Exodus.

Exodus opens with a list of names, Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt, and then the family grows until the land is full of them. Then one quiet, chilling line: a new king arose over Egypt who knew not Joseph. All the grain, all the lives saved, forgotten in a generation. The new king sees this growing people as a threat. He puts them to forced labor, building store cities, making bricks, working the fields. And they keep growing. So he tries something worse, with an order for two women who deliver babies: the first in Exodus to tell Pharaoh no.
screen: `A KING WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH.` → `BRICKS AND FORCED LABOR.` → `AN ORDER FOR TWO MIDWIVES.`

segments.voice: The order: when you help the Hebrew women give birth, if it's a boy, kill him; if it's a girl, let her live. Then the refusal. The text says it simply: "But the midwives feared God." They let the boys live. Fear here isn't panic but reverence: they stood in awe of God more than of the most powerful man they'd ever meet. Then the excuse. Pharaoh calls them back: why have you done this? With a straight face they answer that Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women; they're vigorous, and they give birth before the midwife even gets there. A clever answer, maybe a sly one, and it keeps them alive. Then the names. The midwives are named: Shiphrah and Puah, which the Douay-Rheims spells Sephora and Phua. The king of Egypt never gets a name at all. God dealt well with the midwives, the text says, and gave them households of their own. Nobody knows for sure whether they were Hebrew women or Egyptian women who served the Hebrews; the Hebrew can be read either way. The Church has long honored this kind of courage. Its Catechism says a citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow orders of civil authorities that go against the moral order. Peter put it in one line in Acts: "We ought to obey God, rather than men." Two women in a birthing room said it first. The chapter ends darkly: Pharaoh orders every newborn boy thrown into the Nile.
screen: `IF IT'S A BOY, KILL HIM.` · `BUT THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD.` · `THEY'RE QUICK; WE COME TOO LATE.` · `THE MIDWIVES ARE NAMED. PHARAOH ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Most of us will never face a Pharaoh, but small orders come all day: pass along the rumor, fudge the number, laugh at the joke about someone who isn't there, look away. Picture one you're likely to meet, then picture yourself quietly not doing it, just a no. If you pray, ask for the midwives' kind of courage; if you don't, rehearse that no until it feels like your own.
The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God more than Pharaoh, and let the Hebrew boys live. Today's word.
Your line: two women said no. The king gets no name; they do. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 367 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BASKET IN THE REEDS.`

howItsDone: Catholic teaching on conscience holds that a person must refuse a command from any authority that would require a grave wrong, and Catholic writers on the defense of life often point to Shiphrah and Puah as early examples.

original.note: Hebrew: Shiphrah, a name often explained as beautiful or fair. the Douay-Rheims spells her Sephora.

chat.says: Who were the first people in Exodus to stand up to Pharaoh?
options: Two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah: they feared God and let the baby boys live.
Moses and Aaron, when they walked into his court and said let my people go.
Pharaoh's own daughter, when she pulled a Hebrew baby out of the Nile.
chat.meaning: Ordered to kill the Hebrew boys, the midwives feared God more than the king and let them live. They are named; Pharaoh never is.

Shiphrah.meaning: one of the two midwives who refused Pharaoh

Puah.meaning: the other midwife who let the boys live

Exodus.meaning: the Bible's second book; the name means going out

Acts.meaning: the Acts of the Apostles, the book after the Gospels
